_note: Plain lines before the plain-voice pass (Rule 0c), for comparison and for going back.

cl_aya_dmt_entities.q: What do people say they meet on DMT?
cl_aya_dmt_entities.short: People who said they met a being on DMT mostly called it a 'being', 'guide', 'spirit' or 'alien'. People who said they met 'God' without drugs told similar stories.
cl_aya_dmt_entities.but: Only people who said they met a being or 'God' took part, so we can't tell how often this happens.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people who said they met a being on DMT, in one survey:
pairs: said it gave them a message
freq.note: 2,561 adults recruited online in 2018, each describing their most memorable meeting after smoking or vaping DMT; only people who reported a meeting took part.

how: In 2018, 2,561 adults described their most memorable meeting after smoking or vaping DMT. They were found mainly on DMT and drug websites.
On DMT, most said the being seemed conscious, intelligent and kind. Still, 41 in 100 felt fear at some point.
Not just DMT: of 809 people who said they met 'God' without drugs, 86 in 100 called it kind; 78 in 100 reported a message.
28 in 100 recalled being atheists before DMT and 10 in 100 after. Without drugs, the share fell too. 'Before' was recalled years later.
cl_aya_dmt_entities.rate: Two online surveys from one research team, of people who said they met a being or 'God', looking back years later. Only such people took part, and nothing was measured beforehand.

cl_ket_near_death.q: Do people describe ketamine trips the way others describe near-death experiences?
cl_ket_near_death.short: Of 165 drugs, ketamine trip reports used words most like accounts of near-death experiences. Salvia and LSD came close behind.
cl_ket_near_death.but: Only words were compared. Nobody showed the trips and the near-death experiences feel alike.
how: Researchers took about 15,000 drug reports from the Erowid website. A computer compared their words with 625 near-death accounts.
With the main settings, ketamine came first. Averaged over all settings tried, it led LSD only narrowly, and other drugs swapped places.
The near-death accounts were written about 20 years after the event. Nobody checked what the online writers took, or how much.
Some think a brain chemical like ketamine causes near-death experiences. The authors say their study cannot show that.
cl_ket_near_death.rate: One study comparing words in reports people chose to post online with near-death accounts written years later. Nobody checked the drugs, and ketamine's lead over LSD was small.

cl_psi_mystical.q: Can psilocybin bring on a mystical experience, and does it last?
cl_psi_mystical.short: In a Johns Hopkins study, most volunteers given psilocybin scored as having a 'complete' mystical experience. Two months later, 67 in 100 ranked it among their 5 most meaningful experiences.
cl_psi_mystical.but: Everyone in the psilocybin study took part in religious or spiritual activities; the authors say that may have made them see it as more spiritual.

freq.what: volunteers ranked their psilocybin session among the 5 most meaningful experiences of their lives, 2 months later
compare: after methylphenidate (a stimulant used for comparison)
freq.note: One study: 16 of 24 after psilocybin, 2 of 24 after methylphenidate (counted from a figure). All took part in religious or spiritual activities.

how: At Johns Hopkins, 36 healthy people new to psychedelics took part. 30 got psilocybin once and a stimulant once, 2 months apart, in random order.
'Mystical' meant high questionnaire scores for unity and sacredness: 19 of 30 on psilocybin. A trial in people with drinking problems also found high scores.
Two months after psilocybin, most said it had changed them for the better; people close to them saw small changes. Personality and mood tests didn't.
On psilocybin, 11 of 36 felt strong or extreme fear at some point, and 3 said they'd never want to repeat it.
cl_psi_mystical.rate: The lasting part comes from one study of 24 religious or spiritual volunteers rating their own psilocybin sessions. Another trial found high scores during sessions, but almost everyone guessed which pill they got.

cl_mdma_feelings.short: Compared with a dummy pill, lab MDMA felt good for hours, with unwanted effects too.
cl_mdma_feelings.but: Lab volunteers were healthy and had researchers with them; the one study at a real club was small, with no dummy pill.
how: In the biggest set of lab studies (166 healthy adults), the good effect was rated about 80 out of 100, against 3 or 4 after a dummy pill. It began in about half an hour and lasted about four hours. Looking back, 67 in 100 called it positive and 15 in 100 disappointing or bad.

The same sessions brought unwanted effects, like less appetite, a dry mouth or a clenched jaw. Some felt little: for some the start was slow, and an antidepressant given first cut the effect. Nobody took more, so that was not tested.

At a London club, people who took ecstasy felt about as good as other clubbers, most of whom were drinking. Two days later they felt sadder and less sociable than the others. A week later they felt like the others again.

In the club study, people chose their own drugs, nobody checked what was in the pills, and people rated their own moods knowing what the study was about. So it shows what they felt, not what MDMA alone did.
cl_mdma_feelings.rate: Lab trials in which 166 healthy volunteers each got both MDMA and a dummy pill; the gap was very large, and four places agree. Most could tell which they got, though.

cl_mdma_response_predictors.q: Do some people feel MDMA more strongly than others?
cl_mdma_response_predictors.short: In lab studies, how strong MDMA felt went most with the amount per kilo of body weight.
cl_mdma_response_predictors.but: Healthy young volunteers in a hospital, most trying MDMA for the first time.
how: 194 healthy young adults took MDMA in hospital, one set amount each time. On another day they took a dummy pill.

The amount for each kilo of body weight went most with how strong it felt. Women and men did not clearly differ once weight was counted. An earlier report from the same lab suggested women may feel more bad effects.
People who tend to worry, or who felt anxious and low just before, said they felt more anxious than calm people did. Open people felt closer to others.
Each session had one fixed amount, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested.
cl_mdma_response_predictors.rate: A pooled set of 10 studies from one lab, with 194 healthy volunteers. It compares people who differ in many ways, and each trait was checked on its own, not alongside the others.

cl_mdma_side_effects_reviews.short: In trials, MDMA often caused side effects such as a tight jaw, worry, less appetite or feeling sick, mostly gone within a week.
cl_mdma_side_effects_reviews.but: Many trials only noted problems people mentioned themselves, some recorded problems were left out of the published papers, and there is too little information on what happens later.
how: These effects were more common than with a dummy pill or a very small dose.
In one small trial in people with a serious illness, 11 of 13 on MDMA had a tight jaw, against 1 of 5 on a dummy pill.
One review found one serious problem linked to MDMA: extra heartbeats the person already had became more frequent and needed a night of monitoring in hospital.
Of the problems listed in trial records, more than half of the minor ones and 4 serious ones, all in people on MDMA, never made it into the published papers.
cl_mdma_side_effects_reviews.rate: Reviews pooling 8 trials with 298 people, mostly PTSD trials from one sponsor. Staff noting side effects probably knew who got MDMA, and few trials looked beyond PTSD.

cl_xc_afterglow.short: Studies often found less low mood and stress than before, and more wellbeing; some people had headaches or slept badly.
cl_xc_afterglow.but: Most studies had no blinded placebo group, and most took place in labs or ceremonies with support, not at parties or at home.
how: A review collected 48 studies of psilocybin, LSD, ayahuasca and similar drugs.
People filled in the same questionnaires before, and again in the days or weeks after.
Most studies that measured it found less depression and stress, and more wellbeing, than before.
In studies that looked for problems, headaches were most common, and one person had a severe worsening of anxiety.
cl_xc_afterglow.rate: 48 studies, most without a dummy-pill comparison, in supportive settings. The review only counted which studies found a change, not how big, and side effects were reported unevenly.

cl_gen_release_deaths.q: Is the risk of dying highest just after leaving prison?
cl_gen_release_deaths.short: In one large study, the risk of dying was highest 2 to 7 days after release.
cl_gen_release_deaths.but: The records did not name the drugs, and no one measured tolerance.
how: Researchers used death records for about 1.5 million people who left prison or jail. They lived in eight countries, from 1980 to 2018.
16 of the 18 groups had records for each day. In them, the risk of dying in days 2 to 7 after release was about 1.5 to 2 times the risk in later weeks.
Poisoning by alcohol or other drugs was the most common recorded cause of death, in that first week and overall. But 91 in 100 of these deaths happened more than 4 weeks after release.
The study had no information on drug use, treatment or tolerance. So it cannot say why the first week is riskier.
cl_gen_release_deaths.rate: Death records of 1,471,526 people released from prison or jail in eight countries, all analysed the same way. But it is one study, and how causes were recorded wasn't checked.

cl_meth_acute_toxicity.short: Meth poisoning can look like a body in overdrive: a racing heart, fast breathing, being very restless and upset.
cl_meth_acute_toxicity.but: This comes from reviews of hospital studies. How often each sign appears differs a lot between them.
how: Signs include a racing heart, high blood pressure, fast breathing and wide pupils. People can be very restless and upset.
The body can get very hot. Chest pain and organ failure can happen, and some people die.
This comes from two reviews of hospital studies; how often each sign appears differs a lot.
Neither review says how many patients die.
cl_meth_acute_toxicity.rate: Two reviews of hospital records and case reports; the original studies could not be checked through them. Some of those studies were about amphetamine or other stimulants, not meth.

cl_mix_opioid_tolerance_loss.short: Two reviews say tolerance to opioids may fall after a break from using them.
cl_mix_opioid_tolerance_loss.but: The reviews give no numbers: not how long a break must be, nor how much risk changes.
how: After a break, a dose that used to feel usual might have a much stronger effect, including on breathing.
The main study behind this idea looked at hair samples from people who died of heroin overdose.
One review gives prison and detox as examples of a break. The review it cites does not.
Two studies of people on methadone found tolerance to its effect on breathing was not complete.
cl_mix_opioid_tolerance_loss.rate: Two reviews, one citing the other, describing a few older studies. The original studies couldn't be checked, and the key one, the review itself says, only hints at this.

cl_opi_naloxone_programs.q: Does giving out naloxone kits prevent opioid overdose deaths?
cl_opi_naloxone_programs.short: Naloxone kits are linked to fewer deaths from heroin and other opioids, but it's not proven. At least 96 in 100 people given naloxone by someone trained survived.
cl_opi_naloxone_programs.but: Surviving doesn't prove naloxone saved a life, since most overdoses aren't fatal, and only one study compared death rates.
how: In 19 Massachusetts towns, 2006 to 2009, 2,912 people who might see an opioid overdose got training and nasal naloxone. They reported 327 rescue attempts.
Where over 1 in 1,000 people were trained, opioid death rates were about a fifth lower, and about half after allowing for other differences.
Every town had the programme by 2008, so the study mostly compared later years with earlier ones. It never printed how many people died.
Trained people gave naloxone 2,336 times, mostly for heroin overdoses; 20 are known to have died. Since most overdoses aren't fatal, lives saved are unknown.
cl_opi_naloxone_programs.rate: No fair test exists: the one death-rate study mostly compared later years with earlier ones in 19 Massachusetts towns, and the other studies only counted who survived, which can't show lives saved.

cl_opi_using_alone.q: How common is using drugs alone, and why do people do it?
cl_opi_using_alone.short: About 3 in 4 people at harm reduction sites had used alone that week. The top reason was comfort at home.
cl_opi_using_alone.but: It was one survey in one part of Canada. Everyone asked already went to these sites.
how: In 2018, 414 people at 27 sites in British Columbia, Canada, did a short survey. The sites hand out safer-use supplies.
Of those who used alone, 44 in 100 said using at home was easier and more comfortable; 14 in 100 did not want others to know. Some wrote that they had no one to use with.
People who used alone were more often without a steady home than people who did not.
The survey could not show if using alone changes overdose risk. It cites coroners' reports. They found that about 7 in 10 people who died of an overdose there in 2016 and 2017 were using alone.

freq.what: had used drugs alone at least once in the past week
freq.note: 314 of 414 people at 27 harm reduction sites in British Columbia, Canada, in 2018.

cl_opi_using_alone.rate: One survey of 414 people who happened to visit harm reduction sites in British Columbia in 2018. 'Alone' was never defined for them, and reasons were picked from a short list.

cl_aya_ceremony_setting.q: Does the kind of ayahuasca ceremony matter for how it goes?
cl_aya_ceremony_setting.short: People who felt safe and supported at their last ceremony recalled a little less fear.
cl_aya_ceremony_setting.but: One survey: people rated the ceremony and how it went at the same time, looking back.
how: Almost 7,000 people who had drunk ayahuasca answered one online survey about their last ceremony.
Those who felt safer and better supported recalled a little less fear, and fewer problems in the weeks after, than those who felt less so.
More traditional practices, and drinking in Amazon countries other than Brazil, went with more fear; church hymns or sermons with less.
Fasting showed no link the study could detect with fear or later problems. All the differences were small, and nothing was measured before people drank.
cl_aya_ceremony_setting.rate: One large survey, recruited through the groups whose ceremonies were rated. People rated the ceremony and how it went at the same sitting, looking back, so each answer could colour the other.

cl_ket_music.short: In one small trial, the top blood pressure number rose less with music.
cl_ket_music.but: Just 32 patients in hospital; the report gave no results on how the sessions felt.
how: 32 patients with hard-to-treat depression had a course of up to six ketamine drips in hospital. Some were picked at random to hear music during each drip; the rest heard none.
With music, the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less during each drip.
The report we read gives no results on how the sessions felt or whether depression improved.
Earlier, a review found 14 studies of music with ketamine, mostly with other medicines during surgery or tests. It found no study comparing music with no music in ketamine treatment for depression.
cl_ket_music.rate: One trial of 32 patients, which measured only blood pressure, not how sessions felt. Other studies are small, mostly during medical procedures, often in children, and known only through a review.

cl_xc_mindset_before.short: Feeling calm and ready beforehand went with easier trips; feeling anxious went with more anxiety.
cl_xc_mindset_before.but: These are links: no study we read changed how people felt beforehand to test it.
how: About 650 people planning their own trip answered surveys; about 200 answered enough to be counted. Those who felt calm, open and ready the day before said the trip was less hard.
In lab studies of LSD, feeling anxious before the dose went with more anxiety. Feeling well went with stronger effects overall, not easier ones.
Bigger links come from people remembering their mood afterwards, and memories can be coloured by how the trip went.
Clinical trials prepare people with meetings and advice. But a review of 25 trials found none that compared different ways of preparing.
cl_xc_mindset_before.rate: One online study of about 198 people planning their own trip, and one lab study. The online study lost about 70% of those who signed up and didn't allow for which drug people took.

cl_xc_music.short: Patients said music shaped their sessions; two kinds of music made no clear difference.
cl_xc_music.but: None of the studies we read compared music with silence, and the trial of two kinds of music had only 10 people.
how: 19 patients with hard-to-treat depression took psilocybin in a clinic with music. Almost all said it helped at times; about half said it sometimes made things harder.
Patients who spoke more warmly about the music had a bigger drop in depression a week later. But both were measured at the same time.

In a trial of 10 people trying to quit smoking, each had one session with classical music and one with gongs and singing bowls, in random order. How mystical or hard the sessions felt did not clearly differ.
In a US survey, people who linked their hardest time to the music did not rate it as harder than others did.
cl_xc_music.rate: One small trial of 10 people compared two playlists, not music with silence, and everyone knew which music played. The rest is what people said afterwards.

cl_xc_setting_support.short: In surveys, feeling safe and supported went with fewer difficult moments, by small amounts.
cl_xc_setting_support.but: People rated this looking back; the one study that asked beforehand found only a weak link.
how: In a study that asked the day before, feeling good about the place and people went with slightly easier trips, but the link was weak and could be chance.
Among almost 7,000 people who drank ayahuasca, those who felt safer and better supported at the ceremony reported a little less fear than others.
In a US survey, people who blamed a lack of support for their hardest trip said it was harder than people who did not.

No study we read put people in different places, or with different people, on purpose to compare them. A review of 25 clinical trials found none either, and the trials set up their rooms and staff in very different ways.
cl_xc_setting_support.rate: Four studies, mostly surveys of people who chose to answer and rated everything afterwards. Results differ by what was asked: blaming the people around showed no link with how hard trips were.

cl_lsd_emergency.q: How often do people seek emergency treatment after LSD?
cl_lsd_emergency.short: About 10 in 1,000 people who had used LSD in the past year said they sought emergency treatment, in one big online survey. After magic mushrooms: 2 in 1,000.
cl_lsd_emergency.but: Volunteers answered an online survey about themselves; nobody checked their answers, or whether the drug was really LSD.

freq.what: people who had used LSD in the past year said they sought emergency treatment afterwards
freq.note: Global Drug Survey 2017, online volunteers: 102 of 10,293 for LSD and 19 of 9,233 for magic mushrooms, all self-reported.

how: In the 2017 Global Drug Survey, 10,293 people who had used LSD in the past year answered this question; 102 said yes.
Most of the 102 had panic, anxiety or confusion; 21 reported thoughts or acts of self-harm, and about half said they were admitted to hospital.
Of about 98 who said how long it lasted, 58 felt back to normal within a day; 11 still had problems after 4 weeks.
People with a past mental health diagnosis reported seeking emergency treatment more often: 1.8 in 100, against 0.7 in 100.
cl_lsd_emergency.rate: One online survey of volunteers in 2016–17, who reported on themselves. Nobody checked hospital records or whether the drug was really LSD, and people who could not answer are missing.

cl_psi_emergency.q: How often do people seek emergency treatment after magic mushrooms?
cl_psi_emergency.short: About 2 in 1,000 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year said they sought emergency treatment, in one big online survey. After LSD: 10 in 1,000.
cl_psi_emergency.but: Volunteers answered an online survey about themselves; nobody checked their answers, and people who could not answer were not counted.

freq.what: people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year said they sought emergency treatment afterwards
freq.note: Global Drug Survey 2017, online volunteers: 19 of 9,233 for magic mushrooms and 102 of 10,293 for LSD, all self-reported.

how: In the 2017 Global Drug Survey, 9,233 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year answered this question; 19 said yes.
Of the 19, 13 reported panic and 13 paranoia; 8 said they were admitted to hospital.
17 of the 18 who answered felt back to normal within a day, and all within a week.
Those who sought treatment were younger: typically 19, against 23 for the others who answered.
cl_psi_emergency.rate: One online survey of volunteers in 2016–17, who reported on themselves. Nobody checked hospital records or what they took, people who could not answer are missing, and only 19 described what happened.

cl_xc_difficult_how_common.q: How often are psychedelic trips difficult, and can problems last?
cl_xc_difficult_how_common.short: 41 in 100 people who had used psychedelics recalled at least one difficult trip.
cl_xc_difficult_how_common.but: One online survey, looking back over a whole life, using questions borrowed from meditation research.
how: 613 US adults who had ever used a psychedelic answered one online survey in 2021, looking back over their whole life.
Most were glad they had used psychedelics: 79 in 100 agreed, at least a little.
In the days or weeks after their hardest trip, 7 in 100 had thoughts of hurting themselves or others, or tried to.
57 in 100 said worry, poor sleep or a similar problem lasted days, but people who had not used psychedelics were not asked.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people who had ever used a psychedelic, in one US online survey:
pairs: said they had had at least one difficult experience
said one had severely affected their ability to get through daily life
sought medical or psychological help afterwards
freq.note: 613 US adults asked once, in 2021, looking back over their whole life (251, 28 and 16 people). No one who had not used psychedelics was asked.

cl_xc_difficult_how_common.rate: One online survey of 613 US adults from a sign-up panel, matched on only sex, age and ethnicity. Its borrowed questions gave counts that disagree, and no comparison group answered them.

cl_can_legal_teens.q: Did teen cannabis use rise after US states legalised it?
cl_can_legal_teens.short: Not in one big US study. After states made recreational cannabis legal, teens in school were a bit less likely to say they had used it in the past month.
cl_can_legal_teens.but: Just 7 states had surveys from both before and after the change, and only for its first few years.
how: Surveys gathered 1.4 million answers from US high school students, 1993 to 2017. Each state was compared before and after its law, against other states.
After recreational laws, the odds of past-month cannabis use were 8% lower. That is not 8 fewer teens in 100, but at most about 2.
Laws for medical cannabis, in 27 states and Washington, DC, were not linked to teen use either way, once other things were counted.
The authors suggest shops that check age make cannabis harder for teens to get. Their source: a 2012 news article. The study didn't test it.
cl_can_legal_teens.rate: Surveys in US schools, not a fair test. Only 7 states had legal cannabis with surveys before and after, no one checked if they were already changing, and other studies were mixed.

cl_can_secondhand_test.q: Can other people's cannabis smoke make you fail a urine drug test?
cl_can_secondhand_test.short: Rarely at the US government's workplace limit: after an hour in thick cannabis smoke, 1 of 18 people who didn't smoke went over it. At a lower limit, 12 did.
cl_can_secondhand_test.but: One small lab test with thick smoke in a sealed room; everyday smoke was not tested.
how: In a sealed room about 3 by 4 metres, 6 people smoked cannabis freely for an hour. 6 people who didn't smoke sat between them.
Only 1 of 250 urine samples went over the US government's workplace limit. It did so on just 1 of 5 labs' tests.
Some private tests use a lower limit. There, 3 to 7 of the 18 would have had a positive that a lab check confirmed.
A positive is a urine result: a THC breakdown product above a set level. It is not a measure of being high.
cl_can_secondhand_test.rate: One lab experiment: 18 people, 6 in each of three settings, sat beside people smoking in a sealed room, in thick smoke in two of them. Everyday exposure was not tested.

cl_gen_deaths_level_changes.short: Yes. Levels can rise or fall and differ between blood vessels.
cl_gen_deaths_level_changes.but: These studies cannot predict the change in one ordinary death.
how: Four selected overdose deaths showed large differences between blood vessels. A medicine given in hospital varied less.
In one person, all imipramine samples after death were about 2 to 8 times the earlier hospital level.
A collection of published reports and Finnish records found that the gap between body samples differs by drug.
Repeated tests found rises for some drugs and falls for others. The first sample was often taken hours after death.
cl_gen_deaths_level_changes.rate: Four overdose deaths picked as examples, and 5,375 cases gathered mostly from published reports, without showing how much results vary. Some evidence on changes after death comes from animals.

cl_gen_portugal.q: What happened after Portugal decriminalised all drugs?
cl_gen_portugal.short: In 2001 Portugal stopped treating having any drug for your own use, even heroin, as a crime. Drug use rose slightly; new HIV cases in people who use drugs fell.
cl_gen_portugal.but: Treatment and other help for people who use drugs grew from 1999, so these figures cannot show what the law alone did.

freq.what: adults (aged 15 to 64) in Portugal said in 2007 that they had ever used an illegal drug
freq.note: National surveys: 7.8 in 100 in 2001 (7.6 in the paper's table) and 12.0 in 2007. Use in the past year: 3.4 and 3.7 in 100.

how: Adults who had ever tried an illegal drug rose from about 8 to 12 in 100 (2001 to 2007); past-year use barely changed.
New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell from 907 (2000) to 267 (2008). The paper says this has been credited mainly to more harm reduction services, without saying by whom.
Deaths doctors judged drug-caused fell from about 76 to 20 (2001 to 2008). Deaths with drugs found fell, then rose as testing more than doubled.
Crime arrests for drugs fell from over 14,000 to 5,000–5,500 a year, mostly because possession stopped counting as a crime.
cl_gen_portugal.rate: National statistics before and after the law in one country, loosely compared with Spain and Italy. Treatment grew at the same time, and some counts changed method. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_opi_poppy_seeds.q: Can eating poppy seeds make you fail a sports drug test?
cl_opi_poppy_seeds.short: In one study, yes: all 9 people who ate poppy seed cake had morphine, an opioid, in their urine above the sports limit.
cl_opi_poppy_seeds.but: The cake used the strongest of 8 seed products tested. It had about 18 to 250 times more morphine than the rest.
how: Researchers in Germany tested 8 poppy seed products from shops and a bakery. All held some morphine; one held far more than the rest.
9 volunteers ate cake made with that one. Every person's urine went over the sports limit in at least 2 samples.
One of the 9 was still above the limit about 2 days later; the other 8 had their last positive within a day.
Only the sports limit was checked; workplace tests were not studied. A positive is a urine result, not a measure of any effect.
cl_opi_poppy_seeds.rate: One small study: 9 volunteers, one very morphine-rich batch of seeds, no comparison cake and no urine sample before eating. Workplace tests were not checked.

cl_dc_benzo_strips.short: Often not. At one drug-checking service, strips missed 9 of 24 samples with newer benzodiazepines.
cl_dc_benzo_strips.but: A lab checked only some samples. Many were picked because of a suspected overdose.
how: At eight health sites, samples were tested with strips, and a lab checked some of them.
Strips showed newer benzodiazepines in 15 of 24 samples, but in only 8 of 16 with etizolam alone.
They also read positive in 20 of 129 samples in which the lab found none.
In a lab, the same maker's strip never reacted to pure etizolam. An earlier report said similar strips seemed to pick it up in larger amounts, so the two disagree.

freq.what: samples with a newer benzodiazepine showed it on the strip
freq.note: 15 of 24 samples at one drug-checking service, 2018 to 2020. With etizolam alone, 8 of 16.

cl_dc_benzo_strips.rate: One brand of urine strip, tried at one Canadian drug-checking programme and on pure samples in a lab. Only 159 of 1368 samples were lab-checked, and those were not picked at random.

cl_dc_fts_detects_fentanyl.short: In lab tests, strips found fentanyl in 104 of 106 drug samples that had it.
cl_dc_fts_detects_fentanyl.but: Lab staff did these tests, mostly with one brand. Testing at home was not studied.
how: Two labs tested strips on 106 police-seized drug samples that had fentanyl. The strips showed it in 104.
A lab machine had already found fentanyl in all of these samples. Samples with very little fentanyl were not tested this way.
Strips can find very small amounts of fentanyl. But the smallest amount found differed up to 25 times between studies and batches.
It also depended on how a faint line was read. Trained staff did all of these tests.

freq.what: seized samples with fentanyl showed it on the strip
freq.note: 104 of 106 police-seized samples in which a lab machine had already found fentanyl. One brand, read by trained staff in two labs, 2017.

cl_dc_fts_detects_fentanyl.rate: Teams in five labs agree. But the main check sorted 210 drug samples with a lab test that spots traces less well than the strip, so samples with only traces were left out.

cl_dc_home_vs_service.short: For opioids, about the same. For meth and cocaine, take-home strips showed fentanyl far more often.
cl_dc_home_vs_service.but: The two groups tested different samples, and no lab checked which results were right.
how: In 2019, people took strips from ten health sites and used them at home a little over half the time. Staff tested other samples at the sites.
Opioids: 90 in 100 take-home results showed fentanyl, and 89 in 100 on site.
Crystal meth: 28 in 100 take-home results, and 5 in 100 on site. The authors think most of the extra take-home positives were false.
People told the study their own results, often from memory.

freq.title: Out of every 100 crystal meth samples, how many showed fentanyl?
pairs: tested by the person with a take-home strip
tested on site by trained staff
freq.note: 73 of 265 and 5 of 97 samples, British Columbia, 2019. Different samples; no lab checked which results were right.

cl_dc_home_vs_service.rate: One study in British Columbia in 2019 compared results people recorded themselves with staff results on different samples. People chose which result sheets to hand back, and many readings were recalled later.

cl_dc_nitazene_strips.short: In lab tests, the strips found most nitazenes. They missed most of one group, called desnitazenes.
cl_dc_nitazene_strips.but: Only pure or nearly pure drugs were tested. Mixed street drugs were not.
how: One lab tested 33 nitazenes. The strips showed 24 of them. They missed 6 of the 7 desnitazenes, even in large amounts.
Six nearly pure powders from the drug market all showed up.
A second lab found the strips did not react to 76 other drugs and cutting agents.
No study tested street drugs where a nitazene is a small part of a mix.
cl_dc_nitazene_strips.rate: Two labs tested one brand of strip on pure or nearly pure samples in water, not messy street drugs. Most kinds of nitazene were tested with just one strip per strength.

cl_dc_xylazine_strips.short: Strips found xylazine in 37 of 38 samples with enough of it, but often missed small amounts.
cl_dc_xylazine_strips.but: One batch of strips was read in a lab. The samples were residues from used equipment, not powders.
how: A lab tested 100 residue samples wiped from used syringes, bags and pill bottles, and checked them with a lab machine.
With enough xylazine, 37 of 38 read positive. With less, only 6 of 28 did. None of 34 without xylazine read positive.
In pure water, every strip read positive only from 2.5 times the amount the strip is made to find.
Lidocaine, a common cutting agent, also made strips positive. At the one amount tested, they did not react to medetomidine. It is a similar drug used on animals.

freq.title: Out of every 100 samples with xylazine, how many read positive?
pairs: samples with at least the amount the strip is made to find
freq.note: 37 of 38 and 6 of 28 residue samples, one batch of strips, read in a lab.

cl_dc_xylazine_strips.rate: Two lab studies by one team. The main figure leaves out samples with only a little xylazine, and the study doesn't say how samples were chosen or whether strip readers knew the right answers.

cl_opi_deaths_heroin_alone.short: Other drugs are often found. That does not show which caused the death.
cl_opi_deaths_heroin_alone.but: These old records cannot tell how many deaths heroin alone caused.
how: In older studies from the USA, Australia and Europe, morphine was the only drug found in 23 to 48 in 100 deaths labelled heroin overdose. Alcohol was found in 29 to 75 in 100.
Many deaths took hours; other people were often present. These are findings relayed by a review.

In England and Wales in 2000, researchers put 23 in 100 reported accidental drug-related deaths in categories beyond direct overdose, under their rules. Methadone was the only drug blamed in 4 in 100 direct overdoses; that does not mean no other drug was found.
Heroin exposure may also be missed when its marker breaks down. Blood levels also depend on the specimen and sampling time.
cl_opi_deaths_heroin_alone.rate: Old death records, mostly from 1967–1996, retold by a review that did not check its studies, plus one register from England and Wales in 2000. Neither describes today's drug supply.

cl_meth_mechanism_release.short: It makes nerve cells let out three brain chemicals: dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin.
cl_meth_mechanism_release.but: How it does this is not fully known. So far we have only read a review about it.
how: Meth makes nerve endings let out dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin.
It seems to push them out of their storage sacs and run their pumps in reverse.
The details are not fully known. This comes from a review; we have not read the lab studies yet.
cl_meth_mechanism_release.rate: Lab and animal studies, known only through one review; the original studies haven't been read yet, so how good they are is unknown.

cl_ket_depression_infusion.q: Can a ketamine drip lift depression within hours, and for how long?
cl_ket_depression_infusion.short: A ketamine drip eased depression within hours: a day later, 64 in 100 were much better, against 28 in 100 on a sedative. For most, it faded within weeks.
cl_ket_depression_infusion.but: People can often tell they got ketamine, which may make the lift look bigger.

freq.what: were much better a day after one ketamine drip
freq.note: One trial at two US research centres, 2010 to 2012: 30 of 47 given ketamine and 7 of 25 given midazolam.

how: In a 2006 trial, 12 of 17 people were much better a day after a ketamine drip. After a salt-water drip, none of 14 were.
In a 2013 trial, 72 people got ketamine or a sedative, picked to make it hard to guess which. Other medicines had failed them.
Pooled trials show the gap is biggest about a day after a ketamine drip. In the 2013 trial, it was not clear by a week.
Two of the 2013 trial's authors were named on patent applications for ketamine in depression. One gave up any share of the money.
cl_ket_depression_infusion.rate: Many trials agree, but people could often tell they got ketamine. Trials that found nothing may also be missing.

cl_mdma_indications_overview.short: Outside PTSD, nobody can yet say whether MDMA therapy helps.
cl_mdma_indications_overview.but: Each condition had at most one very small trial, and people could usually tell whether they had MDMA.
how: Reviews up to 2024 found single small trials in people anxious about a serious illness, autistic adults with social anxiety, and people with tinnitus.
Studies in people with alcohol problems and in couples had no comparison group.
In the serious-illness trial, anxiety fell more with MDMA, but the trial was too small to be sure.
A critical review found that only the two later PTSD trials met its basic standard.
cl_mdma_indications_overview.rate: Outside PTSD, each condition has had one small trial at most, the largest with 18 people. People could usually tell whether they had MDMA and rated their own symptoms.

cl_mdma_ptsd_efficacy.short: With the same therapy, PTSD scores fell more with MDMA than with a dummy pill.
cl_mdma_ptsd_efficacy.but: In the trial that asked, most people knew which pill they had.
how: In two trials run for one sponsor, 194 adults with PTSD had up to three long sessions with MDMA or a dummy pill, plus the same therapy.
About 4 months later, PTSD scores had dropped about 9 to 12 points more with MDMA, on a scale of 0 to 80.
Of those who finished, about 7 in 10 on MDMA no longer had PTSD, against 3 to 5 in 10 on the dummy pill.
Neither trial reports measuring what people expected. The trials report nothing after 4 months, and none we read compared MDMA with standard talking therapy.
cl_mdma_ptsd_efficacy.rate: Two trials of 193 people in all, where chance decided who got MDMA. But most people probably knew which pill they had, and hope or disappointment could explain an unknown part of the difference.

cl_mdma_regulatory_2024.short: In 2024 the US drug regulator said no to MDMA therapy for PTSD.
cl_mdma_regulatory_2024.but: We read the panel's notes, but not the final letter.
how: The regulator's expert panel voted 9 to 2 that the data did not show the treatment works.
It voted 10 to 1 that the benefits did not outweigh the risks.
Panel members worried that people knew which pill they had. They doubted the later check too.
The regulator's own staff said no blood tests were done on treatment days.
cl_mdma_regulatory_2024.rate: The panel's votes come from the regulator's own documents, but the final decision letter was not read, so the decision and its reasons are known mainly from news reports.

cl_mdma_therapy_contested.short: Whether MDMA itself helps PTSD, and for how long, is not settled.
cl_mdma_therapy_contested.but: One sponsor ran both trials, and in the one that asked, most people knew their pill.
how: Two trials found PTSD eased more with MDMA and therapy than with a dummy pill and the same therapy; none tested MDMA against usual talking therapy.
But in the second trial most people could tell which pill they had, and neither trial reports measuring what they expected.
The company's own later check found the gap lasted, but about 3 in 10 people were not checked and some knew their pill.
In 2024 the US regulator said no, and a journal withdrew three earlier studies over rule-breaking at one site.
cl_mdma_therapy_contested.rate: Two trials, where people often knew their pill and rated their own symptoms. Neither compared MDMA with existing therapy or looked beyond 18 weeks. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

cl_psi_addiction.q: Can psilocybin help people drink less?
cl_psi_addiction.short: Maybe. In one trial, people given psilocybin with talk therapy drank heavily on about 10 in 100 days, against 24 with a comparison pill.
cl_psi_addiction.but: Almost everyone could tell if they got psilocybin, and people reported their own drinking.

freq.title: Out of every 100 days in the 8 months after the first dose, how many were heavy-drinking days?
pairs: days for people given psilocybin with talk therapy
days for people given a comparison pill with the same therapy
freq.note: One trial of 93 adults with alcohol use disorder at two US universities: 9.7 against 23.6 in 100 days, as people reported them. Heavy drinking had more than halved in both groups before any pill.

how: At 2 US universities, 93 adults dependent on alcohol were offered 12 talk-therapy sessions. Chance decided who also got psilocybin twice or a comparison pill.
Heavy drinking had already more than halved in both groups during 4 weeks of therapy. That was before any psilocybin or comparison pill.
After about 94 in 100 sessions, people guessed right whether they had psilocybin. So what they expected may explain part of the gap.
cl_psi_addiction.rate: One trial of 93 adults with drinking problems: almost everyone could tell whether they got psilocybin, and they reported their own drinking. It was too small to be sure how big the difference is.

cl_psi_depression.short: In two trials, depression scores fell more after one psilocybin session with two therapists than after a vitamin pill or a tiny dose. This was 3 to 6 weeks later.
cl_psi_depression.but: People could probably tell they had taken psilocybin, and nobody checked, which may have made the gap look bigger.

freq.what: in the psilocybin group had their depression score at least halved at every check, week 1 to week 6
freq.note: One US trial of 104 adults: 20 of 48 against 5 of 44, counting only those checked at every visit.

how: In 10 countries, 233 adults whose depression had resisted 2 to 4 treatments got a full, medium or tiny psilocybin dose.
After 3 weeks, only the full psilocybin dose showed bigger falls in depression than the tiny dose. By 12 weeks the gap could be chance.
In the US, 104 adults got psilocybin or niacin, a vitamin that makes skin flush. Depression scores fell more with psilocybin, through 6 weeks.
In the bigger trial, serious suicidal thoughts or self-harm happened on every dose, more often on higher ones. The US trial recorded none.
cl_psi_depression.rate: Two trials where chance decided who got psilocybin. But people could probably tell whether they had it, nobody checked, and in one, many more dropped out of the vitamin-pill group.

cl_psi_smoking.q: Can psilocybin help people quit smoking?
cl_psi_smoking.short: Not known. In one small study, 12 of 15 people given psilocybin plus lots of counselling weren't smoking 6 months later.
cl_psi_smoking.but: There was no comparison group, so no one can tell what psilocybin added to all the counselling.
how: At Johns Hopkins, 15 adults who had smoked for 31 years on average got 15 weeks of counselling and psilocybin two or three times.
Six months on, breath and urine tests confirmed 12 of 15 given psilocybin weren't smoking. Four of those 12 had smoked again at some point.
The psilocybin paper cites 45 to 59 in 100 not smoking after intensive standard treatment. With so few people, 12 of 15 isn't clearly better.
cl_psi_smoking.rate: One small study: just 15 volunteers, all given psilocybin and lots of counselling, with no comparison group, so nobody can tell what psilocybin itself did.

cl_psi_vs_escitalopram.q: Is psilocybin better than a standard antidepressant for depression?
cl_psi_vs_escitalopram.short: Not shown. In one trial of 59 people, psilocybin and the antidepressant escitalopram showed no clear difference in depression, at 6 weeks or 6 months.
cl_psi_vs_escitalopram.but: The trial was too small to show they work equally well, and people expected nearly twice as much from psilocybin.
how: At one London centre, 59 adults with depression got two psilocybin sessions, or 6 weeks of escitalopram pills plus two tiny psilocybin doses.
After 6 weeks, self-rated depression fell 8 points with psilocybin and 6 with escitalopram, on a 27-point scale: a gap that could be chance.
At 6 weeks, 57 in 100 were nearly free of symptoms with psilocybin and 28 with escitalopram, an extra result the authors drew no conclusions from. Six months on: 37 against 34.
People had higher hopes for psilocybin. Allowing for those hopes, the team found no clear gap on any of six scales.
cl_psi_vs_escitalopram.rate: One small trial of 59 people: too few to tell whether psilocybin and escitalopram work equally well. People rated their own depression, expected more from psilocybin, and by 6 months most had other treatment.

cl_gen_antidrug_ads.q: Did the US government's anti-drug ads stop teens using cannabis?
cl_gen_antidrug_ads.short: No sign they did. Congress put nearly $1 billion into the campaign, but teen cannabis use stayed flat, and teens who remembered more ads weren't less likely to start.
cl_gen_antidrug_ads.but: Nearly every teen saw the ads, so there was no group without them to compare cannabis use with.
how: A national survey interviewed 8,117 US kids aged 9 to 18 at home, and many again up to three times, between 1999 and 2004.
94 in 100 remembered seeing anti-drug ads at least monthly. About 24 in 100 teens had ever used cannabis, in 2000 and again in 2004.
Teens who remembered more ads were no less likely to start cannabis by the next interview, and fewer said they definitely wouldn't.
In one of three periods, more ads even went with more first use of cannabis. The authors call this tentative, not definitive.
cl_gen_antidrug_ads.rate: One national survey followed US teens from 1999 to 2004. Almost every teen saw the ads, so no group without them could be compared, and teens reported their own ad viewing and cannabis use.

cl_gen_dare.q: Did the original DARE school programme stop young people using drugs?
cl_gen_dare.short: No. Across 11 studies of the original DARE school classes, kids who had DARE used alcohol, tobacco and other drugs about as much as kids who didn't.
cl_gen_dare.but: Only the original classes were tested: DARE was rebuilt in 2001, and that version wasn't part of this review.
how: DARE was one of the most used US school drug programmes; the review's authors cite spending of about three quarters of a billion dollars yearly.
A 2004 review combined 11 studies, from 1991 to 2002, comparing students who had DARE with students who didn't.
Students who had DARE used alcohol, tobacco and other drugs about as much as others, from right after the classes to 10 years later.
Two small studies found less use with DARE; the biggest, of 2,878 students, found slightly more. Four results were filled in as zero.
cl_gen_dare.rate: One short review of 11 school studies of the original DARE classes. It did not check how well the studies were done and filled in four results as zero, so its numbers are rough.

cl_gen_deaths_news_stigma.short: In one study, story details changed how harshly readers judged the person who died.
cl_gen_deaths_news_stigma.but: Readers saw one made-up story and answered straight away; nobody checked what they did later.
how: In 2022, 1,248 adults in the UK each read one made-up news story about a drug death, with the details chosen at random.
Readers judged the person more harshly when the person was a man, was older and had used the drug for years, or had taken heroin rather than ecstasy. The differences were small to moderate.
Support for services that reduce harm, such as drug checking, barely changed.
The study could not tell the effect of age apart from the effect of using the drug for longer.
cl_gen_deaths_news_stigma.rate: One online experiment in which chance decided which version of a made-up news story 1,248 UK adults read. The plan was not published first, and the stigma questions were new.

cl_gen_stigma_health_care.q: Do health workers see and treat people who use drugs differently?
cl_gen_stigma_health_care.short: Many health workers said they felt negative. Whether care was worse is not clear.
cl_gen_stigma_health_care.but: Mostly surveys of what workers said, from 2000 to 2011, in a few countries.
how: A review gathered 28 studies, mostly from Australia, the UK and the US. In them, health workers described their views of patients with drug or alcohol problems.

Many workers felt negative about these patients, or less positive than about people with other illnesses. This was more common outside drug and alcohol services. Some studies found neutral or positive views.
Only a few studies asked whether this changes care, and they disagreed. In one, people who felt staff treated them unfairly were less likely to finish treatment.
In another, doctors' views were not linked to what patients said about their care. The one study that watched real visits, from the 1980s, found better care for these patients.
cl_gen_stigma_health_care.rate: One review of 28 papers, mostly surveys of what health workers said, answered by those who chose to. We know them only through the review, whose summaries contain errors.

cl_gen_words_labels_stigma.q: Do words about drug use change how others see a person?
cl_gen_words_labels_stigma.short: In one experiment, people judged 'drug use' more harshly than a 'health concern'.
cl_gen_words_labels_stigma.but: People rated made-up stories. No one checked how people are really treated.
how: 1,613 adults online each read one short story about a person called Alex, with the wording chosen at random. People with a drug or mental health diagnosis, or close family with one, could not take part.

When Alex's trouble was said to come from drug use, not a health concern, readers wanted more distance from Alex. They also saw Alex as more dangerous. In a pretend money task, they took a little more money from Alex, a small difference.
Calling it a 'brain disease' instead of a 'problem' made readers think more that genes or illness caused it. Its other effects were small and unclear.

An older study tested words for the person. About 500 mental health workers at two conferences agreed slightly more that a man deserved blame and punishment when he was called 'a substance abuser' than when he 'has a substance use disorder'. The difference was small and may not be reliable.
cl_gen_words_labels_stigma.rate: A fair test: chance decided which story each of 1,613 online volunteers read. But they answered right after reading, when people may guess what's expected, and many were young.

cl_can_dependence_how_many.q: How many people who use cannabis become dependent on it?
cl_can_dependence_how_many.short: About 9 in 100 people who ever tried it, in two older US surveys.
cl_can_dependence_how_many.but: The surveys are from 1990 to 2005 and used a narrower definition than today's.
how: A US survey in 1990 to 1992 asked about 8,000 people aged 15 to 54 about drug use and dependence.
Of those who had ever used cannabis, even once, about 9 in 100 had been dependent at some point: fewer than for tobacco, heroin, cocaine or alcohol.
A second US survey, in 2001 to 2005, estimated about 9 in 100 over a lifetime; half of those who became dependent did so within about 5 years of first use.
Newer US figures are higher, about 3 in 10, but they count milder cases and only people who used in the past year.

freq.what: of people who had ever used cannabis had been dependent at some point
freq.note: US survey of people aged 15 to 54, 1990 to 1992, with an older, narrower definition of dependence; the tobacco figure was worked out from two surveys.

cl_can_dependence_how_many.rate: Two large US surveys, a decade apart, give almost the same figure. But they asked people in their homes between 1990 and 2005, so other countries and today's cannabis may differ.

cl_coc_crack_powder.q: Is crack more addictive or more harmful than powder?
cl_coc_crack_powder.short: The same drug. People starting crack reported more signs of dependence than people starting powder.
cl_coc_crack_powder.but: Each person was asked once, so the surveys cannot show that crack itself is the reason.
how: Powder can't be smoked; crack is smoked. Smoked or injected cocaine peaks in the blood within minutes, snorted cocaine after about half an hour.
In US surveys from 1995 to 1998, about 18 to 32 in 100 people who had just started crack reported each sign of dependence. For people who had just started powder, it was 5 to 12 in 100.
After allowing for how many days people had used, and for age, drinking, smoking and injecting, the gap was smaller but did not go away.
A review of 302 studies found comparisons of crack with other cocaine mixed. Its authors say crack is not a likely direct cause of the infections and violence linked to it.
cl_coc_crack_powder.rate: US household surveys from 1995–1998 that asked people once, with no way to know how people differed before they started. A review of 302 articles says the wider research disagrees.

cl_coc_dependence_onset.q: How quickly can dependence start after first using cocaine?
cl_coc_dependence_onset.short: Within a year of starting, about 5 in 100 who used only powder were dependent; 22 in 100 who went on to crack.
cl_coc_dependence_onset.but: People answered once, about themselves. The survey cannot show that crack itself made the difference.
how: US surveys from 2002 to 2016 asked people who had first used cocaine less than a year before.
About 5 in 100 of those who had used only powder met the criteria for cocaine dependence, and about 22 in 100 of those who had gone on to crack.
In both groups the most common problem was wanting or trying to cut down or stop: about 45 in 100 and 58 in 100.
People who go on to crack may differ to begin with, and some may already have had problems with powder. The survey did not ask which form caused a problem.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people who had started cocaine in the past year, how many met the criteria for dependence?
pairs: people who had used only powder
people who had also gone on to crack
freq.note: US household surveys, 2002 to 2016. People were asked once, less than a year after they first used cocaine.

cl_coc_dependence_onset.rate: Yearly US surveys from 2002–2016. Only 275 people went on to crack, too few to be sure, and the two groups may have differed before they ever started.

cl_gen_remission.q: Do people recover from drug or alcohol problems, even without treatment?
cl_gen_remission.short: Many do. For alcohol, many people who recovered were never treated.
cl_gen_remission.but: How many depends on who is counted; recovery without treatment was measured only for alcohol.
how: Of US soldiers in Vietnam, 20 in 100 said they had been dependent on narcotics there. In the year after coming home, about 1 in 100 had been. How many had treatment was not counted.
In a US survey, about 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer had enough signs to count as dependent three years later. Some still had a few.

In 20 long studies, mostly of people who had been in treatment, and one survey, 35 to 54 in 100 were in recovery when last seen, about 17 years later on average. The researchers saw this as a slow road for many.

For alcohol, counts of recovery without treatment run from about 3 to 98 in 100, because studies count different groups. Among people who recovered, many were never treated. Among everyone with a drinking problem, fewer recover untreated within a year.

freq.what: adults with alcohol dependence no longer had enough signs to count as dependent about 3 years later
freq.note: US national survey, 2001–2002 and 2004–2005; some still had one or two signs; the editors’ count from the study’s numbers, not weighted, so not a national estimate.

cl_gen_remission.rate: Interviews with soldiers back from Vietnam and a US national survey, plus reviews. Figures on recovery without treatment come second-hand from a review that did not check how good its 27 studies were.

cl_mdma_dependence.short: Some people become dependent on ecstasy. Studies disagree on how many.
cl_mdma_dependence.but: Most studies used volunteers and survey forms made for other drugs, so the numbers may not fit everyone.
how: In two US national surveys, about 4 in 100 people who had used ecstasy recently met the criteria for dependence. In club-goer, detention and volunteer samples, it was 16 to 22 in 100.
Three small samples gave much higher numbers: 43 to 73 in 100 met the criteria at some point in their lives. They included people in drug treatment and people who had taken at least 250 pills.
The one study that followed people found that 93 in 100 of those dependent at the start no longer were after about three years. That group was small: about 12 to 14 people, by our count.

Tolerance means needing more for the same effect. It was among the symptoms people reported most, and it went with using more, or for longer, than meant. Pills sold as ecstasy may hold methamphetamine, so some of this may be dependence on another drug.
cl_mdma_dependence.rate: Studies of 26 to 1,662 people, seen only through one 2010 overview. Who was asked shaped the answer, from 3.6 to 73 in 100, and pills sold as ecstasy may not be MDMA.

cl_meth_dependence_baserate.short: An old US survey asked people who had used stimulants like meth. About 11 in 100 had been dependent at some point.
cl_meth_dependence_baserate.but: Neither survey gives a number for meth alone. The US one also counted people who had only just started.

freq.what: of people who had used stimulants other than cocaine had been dependent at some point
freq.note: US survey, 1990 to 1992: stimulants other than cocaine, not meth alone. Tobacco was measured differently.
freq.compare_k: For comparison, in the same survey:

how: In the early 1990s, a US survey used set interview questions to find who had ever been dependent on a drug they had used.
Stimulants other than cocaine: about 11 in 100. Tobacco 32, alcohol 15, cocaine 17.
It counted people who had just started, so they had little time to become dependent.
An Australian survey asked in a different way. It estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years, also counting a related diagnosis called 'abuse'.
cl_meth_dependence_baserate.rate: Two household surveys, in the US in 1990 to 1992 and Australia in 2007. The US one lumped meth with other stimulants, prescription pills included, and the Australian one never said which stimulants.

cl_mdma_acute_body.short: In a laboratory, one dose of MDMA raised blood pressure, heart rate and temperature.
cl_mdma_acute_body.but: Healthy volunteers rested in a cool room; heat, dancing, crowds, other drugs and extra doses were not tested.
how: In 136 healthy adults given one laboratory dose, the top blood-pressure number went above 160 in 38 in 100 after MDMA, against 6 in 100 after a dummy pill.
A heart rate above 100 happened in 33 in 100 after MDMA, against 2 in 100 after the dummy pill.
Ear temperature went above 38 degrees in 24 in 100 after MDMA, against 9 in 100; the highest was 39.1 degrees.
Four people felt no effect and the study does not say what their bodies did. Everyone got a set dose, so taking more was not tested here.
cl_mdma_acute_body.rate: Nine trials in one Basel lab compared MDMA with dummy pills in the same people, 166 healthy volunteers in all, and machines recorded large changes. But most people could probably tell when they had MDMA.

cl_mdma_hyponatremia.short: Some young people were treated for low blood salt (sodium) after taking MDMA.
cl_mdma_hyponatremia.but: These are reports of people who became ill, so they cannot show how often it happens.
how: In 17 people aged 15 to 26 reported to a UK poisons service, at least 10 had drunk a lot of fluid. Two died; each had taken one tablet, had drunk a lot of water, and drank or was given more after feeling ill.
In California poison-centre records, 73 of 188 people who had their blood salt measured had a low level, and 4 of those 73 died.
The papers think MDMA makes the body hold on to water, which waters down the salt in the blood; the UK authors say how it does this is not yet known.
No paper compared amounts of MDMA or of fluid between people, so none can show whether taking more makes it more likely.
cl_mdma_hyponatremia.rate: Records from two poison services, in the UK and California, which agree. But MDMA was confirmed by tests in only some cases, and in California only about a third had blood salt measured.

cl_mdma_hyponatremia_risk.short: Women with MDMA illness more often had low blood salt than men did.
cl_mdma_hyponatremia_risk.but: These are people who became ill and had a blood test, not everyone who takes MDMA.
how: Of 105 women with a blood salt test, 55 (52 in 100) had a low level; of 83 men, 18 (22 in 100) did.
Women with a low level were also more likely to have fits or coma than women without one; in men the numbers were too small to tell.
A UK group (10 of 17 were women) and a review of published cases (more than 85 in 100 were female) point the same way, but the review's cases overlap with the California ones.

A review describes one controlled study in 8 women and 8 men given the same MDMA amount. A hormone marker rose only in the women; the review does not identify the comparison behind its other hormone and sodium results. This does not establish why women were more common in the reported cases.
cl_mdma_hyponatremia_risk.rate: Records of 188 people at one California poison centre who had blood salt measured. Body size and other differences between women and men were not recorded or allowed for.

cl_mdma_nonlinear.short: A bigger dose of MDMA raised blood levels by more than the dose itself rose.
cl_mdma_nonlinear.but: Only 8 men were compared, in a lab, and the study was not planned to look at this.
how: In 8 men, a dose 1.67 times larger gave a peak blood level 1.8 times higher and about twice the total over the day.
Outside the kidneys, MDMA was cleared about half as fast at the larger dose. The authors read this as slower breakdown in the liver.
The authors suggest the breakdown gets saturated or that MDMA blocks the enzyme that clears it. They also say people may be more prone to acute toxicity; toxicity was not measured.

Feeling little from an amount can come from a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a muting medicine or bodies that differ, and some people take more. These studies gave fixed amounts, so they did not test that.
cl_mdma_nonlinear.rate: One lab trial in which each of 8 men was his own comparison. Blood was tested directly, but this analysis was added afterwards, and with so few men the extra rise could be chance.

cl_mdma_overheating.short: Nobody can yet say why some people get hotter than others with MDMA.
cl_mdma_overheating.but: This is second-hand, from one review of small studies that could not tell heat, dancing and crowds apart.
how: In small lab studies of people at rest, body temperature rose about 0.4 degrees on average at medium doses and 0.7 at higher ones; one person in a group of 8 went up 1.9.
At dance clubs and parties the average rise ran from 0.2 to 1.6 degrees, but the studies compared different things.
In the party studies, the review reports no comparison of amounts, dancing, room heat or crowds, so it cannot say which matters.
People also feel it differently: in one survey, 16 in 100 people who take ecstasy did not feel hot.
cl_mdma_overheating.rate: One overview of small lab and party studies (4 to 41 people) and hospital cases. Each party study used a different comparison, or none, and their results differ widely without explanation.
